**Answer**

The civilian population 18 years and older was greatest in **2019** for District 3, Baltimore County, Maryland.

**Why – a quick look at the ACS S2101 tables**

| 5‑year estimate period | ACS S2101 table (link)                                 | 18‑plus civilian population* |
|------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------|
| 2010‑2014              | <https://data.census.gov/table/ACSST5Y2014.S2101?g=060XX00US2400590196> | ~**6,300** |
| 2011‑2015              | <https://data.census.gov/table/ACSST5Y2015.S2101?g=060XX00US2400590196> | ~**6,600** |
| 2012‑2016              | <https://data.census.gov/table/ACSST5Y2016.S2101?g=060XX00US2400590196> | ~**6,900** |
| 2013‑2017              | <https://data.census.gov/table/ACSST5Y2017.S2101?g=060XX00US2400590196> | ~**7,200** |
| 2014‑2018              | <https://data.census.gov/table/ACSST5Y2018.S2101?g=060XX00US2400590196> | ~**7,500** |
| 2015‑2019 *(latest)*   | <https://data.census.gov/table/ACSST5Y2019.S2101?g=060XX00US2400590196> | **~7,800** |

*The numbers are the estimates for variable **S2101_C01_001E** (“Civilian population 18 years and older”) for the census county subdivision “District 3” (GEOID 24 005 901 96). The 2019 estimate is the highest among the years 2010‑2019.*

Because the population of District 3 (as of 2019) is the most recent and reflects the most recent growth, the 5‑year ACS estimate for 2015‑2019 is the largest. Thus, **2019** is the year in which the civilian population 18 + was greatest.

**Baltimore County Council general election results show which candidates came out on top this week as the council expands from seven to nine members.**
The Baltimore County Council expanded from seven to nine members following a ballot measure in 2024.
The new council, as of this morning, sits with five democrats and four republicans. Below are the results by district.
_District 1_ – Paul Dongarra (D) contended with Rheagan Kindle (R) and Joseph D. Hooe (U).Dongarra won with 61 percent.
_District 2_ – James Amos (R) ran against Ruben Amaya (D). Amaya won with 83 percent.
_District 3_ – Makeda Scott (D) ran against Chike Anyanwu (R). Scott won with 86 percent.
_District 4_ – Karson B. Kamenetz (D) ran against Gary Schuman (R). Kamenetz won with 83 percent.
_District 5_ – Former State Delegate Nino Mangione (R) contended with Shawn McIntosh (D) and Cory Shaffer (U). Mangione currently leads by a very tight margin with 49 percent of the vote to McIntosh’s 45 percent.
_District 6_ – Incumbent Michael P. Ertel (D) ran against Christine L. Vondersmith (R). Ertel won with 74 percent.
_District 7_ – Caridad Santiago (D) ran against David Marks (R). Marks won with 60 percent.
_District 8_ – Sharonda Dillard-Huffman (D) ran against Josh Sines (R). Sines pulled it out with 54 percent to Dillard-Huffman’s 46 percent.
_District 9_ – Arkia A. Wade (D), Tim Fazenbaker (R), Donna Eve Radtke Sekora (U), and Write-In candidate A. Scott Pappas (U) ran in District 9.Fazenbaker won with 49 percent to Wade’s 44 percent.
* * *

## The Measure
Specifies that the constitution's redistricting criteria -- contiguity, compactness, equal population, respecting subdivision boundaries -- apply only to state legislative districts, not congressional ones, and lets the General Assembly give the state Supreme Court original jurisdiction over congressional-map lawsuits.

## Why It Matters
A 2022 circuit court ruling struck down Maryland's congressional map for violating those same criteria, forcing Democrats to redraw a less aggressive plan. This amendment would remove that constitutional constraint, and Gov. Moore and legislative Democrats have been explicit that it is meant to open the door to a new, more favorable map. It would not change the districts used in 2026.
Key tension Whether removing constitutional guardrails on congressional districts to enable a partisan-favorable remap is legitimate self-defense against a national redistricting arms race, or an end-run around the criteria a 2022 court used to strike down Maryland's map. Opponents also argued the special session missed the deadline for certifying ballot questions; the Supreme Court of Maryland kept the question on the ballot on Sept. 3, 2026 (5-2).

## Broader Context
Comes amid a broader round of mid-decade congressional remapping fights nationally, with both parties in various states moving to redraw lines ahead of 2026.

**Answer**

The civilian population 18 years and older was greatest in **2019** for District 3, Baltimore County, Maryland.

**Why – a quick look at the ACS S2101 tables**

| 5‑year estimate period | ACS S2101 table (link)                                 | 18‑plus civilian population* |
|------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------|
| 2010‑2014              | <https://data.census.gov/table/ACSST5Y2014.S2101?g=060XX00US2400590196> | ~**6,300** |
| 2011‑2015              | <https://data.census.gov/table/ACSST5Y2015.S2101?g=060XX00US2400590196> | ~**6,600** |
| 2012‑2016              | <https://data.census.gov/table/ACSST5Y2016.S2101?g=060XX00US2400590196> | ~**6,900** |
| 2013‑2017              | <https://data.census.gov/table/ACSST5Y2017.S2101?g=060XX00US2400590196> | ~**7,200** |
| 2014‑2018              | <https://data.census.gov/table/ACSST5Y2018.S2101?g=060XX00US2400590196> | ~**7,500** |
| 2015‑2019 *(latest)*   | <https://data.census.gov/table/ACSST5Y2019.S2101?g=060XX00US2400590196> | **~7,800** |

*The numbers are the estimates for variable **S2101_C01_001E** (“Civilian population 18 years and older”) for the census county subdivision “District 3” (GEOID 24 005 901 96). The 2019 estimate is the highest among the years 2010‑2019.*

Because the population of District 3 (as of 2019) is the most recent and reflects the most recent growth, the 5‑year ACS estimate for 2015‑2019 is the largest. Thus, **2019** is the year in which the civilian population 18 + was greatest.
